Letta is a practical open-source framework for assistants that need persistent, structured memory across sessions. It is useful for long-running tasks where the agent must remember approved facts, retrieve older context, and respect clear boundaries for retention, deletion, and access.

🧭 Overview
A normal chat request can forget everything when the session ends. Letta gives the assistant an explicit memory layer: read relevant state, reason over the current task, write only validated updates, and carry selected context into the next session. This makes memory inspectable and testable instead of hiding it in an ever-growing prompt.

🛠️ What it does
• Separates durable core memory from searchable archival and recall context.
• Lets an agent read and write structured memory through bounded operations and tools.
• Supports long-running assistants whose behavior evolves across conversations.
• Makes retention, deletion, permissions, and memory inspection part of the system design.

✅ Practical uses
1) Build a personal research assistant that remembers project preferences, approved terminology, and recurring goals without replaying every old transcript.
2) Create a support assistant that keeps a controlled customer profile while retrieving only the records allowed for the current tenant and case.
3) Run a multi-session coding or writing workflow that stores decisions, open questions, and accepted constraints for the next session.
4) Compare memory policies, retrieval limits, and write rules on a fixed task set to learn whether persistence improves completion or only adds stale context.

⚙️ Getting started
Start with one small memory schema and define what belongs in core memory, what belongs in archival storage, and what should never be persisted. Give every memory item an owner, type, timestamp, source, confidence, and access scope. Make writes explicit: an agent should propose a memory update, validate it, then store it through a controlled operation.

Log memory reads, selected items, writes, deletions, retrieval scores, prompt size, latency, and final status. Test conflicting memories, stale preferences, duplicate facts, malformed records, empty recall, a user asking to forget something, and prompt injection inside an archived document. Keep a clear fallback when evidence conflicts: ask the user, prefer the latest approved source, or do not use the memory.

For production prototypes, separate read and write permissions. Add retention rules and a deletion path that covers primary storage, indexes, caches, and backups. Encrypt sensitive memory, redact logs, isolate tenants, and require human approval before a memory update can change a business or safety decision.

⚠️ License & security
Review the current Letta code, dependencies, connector licenses, model terms, and deployment obligations before redistribution or commercial use. Treat user input, stored memories, retrieved documents, tool responses, and model output as untrusted data: validate schemas, enforce access filters, protect credentials, and keep an audit trail of why each memory was read or changed.

When I first saw claude-mem, I thought: another memory layer. We already have mem0, supermemory, Letta and Basic Memory.

Then I dug in. 𝗔 𝗳𝗲𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘂𝗽 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 𝗜𝘁 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲𝘀

You spend an hour with Claude Code. It reads your files, runs the tests, finds the bug, fixes it.

Then you close the session. Tomorrow it knows 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 about that hour.

Here's the surprise: Claude Code does have its own "auto memory". But its docs say it 𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘱𝘴 𝘥𝘦𝘣𝘶𝘨𝘨𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘧𝘪𝘹𝘦𝘴 and anything it can work out from the code. 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁'𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗮𝗽 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲-𝗺𝗲𝗺 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗜𝘁 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀

• 𝗜𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀: hooks fire on the agent's own events, like session start, each prompt and each tool call.
• 𝗜𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀: a model turns what happened into short notes.
• 𝗜𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗲𝘀: the notes go into a SQLite database on your machine, with Chroma for meaning-based search.
• 𝗜𝘁 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸: at the next session start, relevant notes are added to the context.

Search is staged: a short index first (𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟱𝟬–𝟭𝟬𝟬 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻𝘀 per result), then a timeline, then full details (𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟱𝟬𝟬–𝟭,𝟬𝟬𝟬 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻𝘀) only for what matters.

𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲, 𝗦𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀

𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘆: you and the agent spend an hour on a login bug. It reads 𝚊𝚞𝚝𝚑/𝚖𝚒𝚍𝚍𝚕𝚎𝚠𝚊𝚛𝚎.𝚝𝚜, runs the tests, sees 3 failures, finds the token-refresh time was wrong, fixes it. Tests pass.

𝗧𝘂𝗲𝘀𝗱𝗮𝘆: new session. You ask: "The auth test is failing again. What did we change last time?"

What does the agent know?

• CLAUDE.md: 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳. If you didn't write down Monday's fix, it doesn't know.
• Claude Code auto memory: notes about you, your feedback, ongoing project decisions and references. By design it skips debugging fixes, so 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘆'𝘀 𝗳𝗶𝘅 𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲.
• mem0: 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴, unless you're building your own app and your code sends it the conversation. It pulls facts out of what you send. A building block, not a memory plugin for Claude Code.
• supermemory plugin: hooks send your prompt to Supermemory's service (it needs their API key) and add matching memories and a profile of you. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗹.
• Letta Code: 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗮'𝘀 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 instead of Claude Code. It rewrites its own memory, skills and prompts, and tracks its memory in git.
• Basic Memory: Markdown files you and the AI both read and edit through MCP. It knows about Monday if a note was written on Monday.
• claude-mem: 𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘆: the file read, the test run, the failures, the edit. A model turned that into a note like "𝘣𝘶𝘨𝘧𝘪𝘹: 𝘵𝘰𝘬𝘦𝘯 𝘳𝘦𝘧𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘩 𝘪𝘯 𝘮𝘪𝘥𝘥𝘭𝘦𝘸𝘢𝘳𝘦.𝘵𝘴 𝘶𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘪𝘳𝘺". On Tuesday it's added at session start, and the agent can search the timeline.

𝗜𝗻 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁:

• mem0 is 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗮𝗽𝗽.
• Letta Code 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁.
• Basic Memory is 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳.
• supermemory and claude-mem 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗵 𝗽𝗹𝘂𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲. supermemory keeps memory in its cloud service. claude-mem records each tool call and keeps the database on your machine.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗘𝗹𝘀𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗨𝗻𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱

• 𝗜𝘁'𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲: install options for OpenCode, T3 Code, Antigravity CLI, Grok Bot, Pi and DeepSeek Harness, plus plugins for Cursor, Codex and Hermes Agent.
• 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝗽𝘁-𝗶𝗻: agents write to the same project memory, but by default a new session only loads notes from the same agent. One setting changes that.
• 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗴𝗼 𝘁𝗼 𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹: the installer first offers claude-mem's own hosted note-writer (30-day trial). Your own Anthropic, OpenRouter or Gemini key still sends session data to that provider. 𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗵𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹.
• 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗱: the README's "𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟭𝟬𝘅 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀" has no independent test.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗡𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀

𝗔𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟭𝟭𝟭.𝟴𝗸 𝗚𝗶𝘁𝗛𝘂𝗯 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘀 and 9.7k forks as of today. Created August 2025, Apache-2.0, now at v15.9.0. 𝗔𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟵𝟯𝗸 𝗻𝗽𝗺 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗱𝘀 in the last 30 days.

Then I dug in. 𝗔 𝗳𝗲𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘂𝗽 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 𝗜𝘁 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲𝘀

You spend an hour with Claude Code. It reads your files, runs the tests, finds the bug, fixes it.

Then you close the session. Tomorrow it knows 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 about that hour.

Here's the surprise: Claude Code does have its own "auto memory". But its docs say it 𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘱𝘴 𝘥𝘦𝘣𝘶𝘨𝘨𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘧𝘪𝘹𝘦𝘴 and anything it can work out from the code. 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁'𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗮𝗽 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲-𝗺𝗲𝗺 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗜𝘁 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀

• 𝗜𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀: hooks fire on the agent's own events, like session start, each prompt and each tool call.
• 𝗜𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀: a model turns what happened into short notes.
• 𝗜𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗲𝘀: the notes go into a SQLite database on your machine, with Chroma for meaning-based search.
• 𝗜𝘁 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸: at the next session start, relevant notes are added to the context.

Search is staged: a short index first (𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟱𝟬–𝟭𝟬𝟬 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻𝘀 per result), then a timeline, then full details (𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟱𝟬𝟬–𝟭,𝟬𝟬𝟬 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻𝘀) only for what matters.

𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲, 𝗦𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀

𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘆: you and the agent spend an hour on a login bug. It reads 𝚊𝚞𝚝𝚑/𝚖𝚒𝚍𝚍𝚕𝚎𝚠𝚊𝚛𝚎.𝚝𝚜, runs the tests, sees 3 failures, finds the token-refresh time was wrong, fixes it. Tests pass.

𝗧𝘂𝗲𝘀𝗱𝗮𝘆: new session. You ask: "The auth test is failing again. What did we change last time?"

What does the agent know?

• CLAUDE.md: 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳. If you didn't write down Monday's fix, it doesn't know.
• Claude Code auto memory: notes about you, your feedback, ongoing project decisions and references. By design it skips debugging fixes, so 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘆'𝘀 𝗳𝗶𝘅 𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲.
• mem0: 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴, unless you're building your own app and your code sends it the conversation. It pulls facts out of what you send. A building block, not a memory plugin for Claude Code.
• supermemory plugin: hooks send your prompt to Supermemory's service (it needs their API key) and add matching memories and a profile of you. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗹.
• Letta Code: 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗮'𝘀 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 instead of Claude Code. It rewrites its own memory, skills and prompts, and tracks its memory in git.
• Basic Memory: Markdown files you and the AI both read and edit through MCP. It knows about Monday if a note was written on Monday.
• claude-mem: 𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘆: the file read, the test run, the failures, the edit. A model turned that into a note like "𝘣𝘶𝘨𝘧𝘪𝘹: 𝘵𝘰𝘬𝘦𝘯 𝘳𝘦𝘧𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘩 𝘪𝘯 𝘮𝘪𝘥𝘥𝘭𝘦𝘸𝘢𝘳𝘦.𝘵𝘴 𝘶𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘪𝘳𝘺". On Tuesday it's added at session start, and the agent can search the timeline.

𝗜𝗻 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁:

• mem0 is 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗮𝗽𝗽.
• Letta Code 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁.
• Basic Memory is 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳.
• supermemory and claude-mem 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗵 𝗽𝗹𝘂𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲. supermemory keeps memory in its cloud service. claude-mem records each tool call and keeps the database on your machine.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗘𝗹𝘀𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗨𝗻𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱

• 𝗜𝘁'𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲: install options for OpenCode, T3 Code, Antigravity CLI, Grok Bot, Pi and DeepSeek Harness, plus plugins for Cursor, Codex and Hermes Agent.
• 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝗽𝘁-𝗶𝗻: agents write to the same project memory, but by default a new session only loads notes from the same agent. One setting changes that.
• 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗴𝗼 𝘁𝗼 𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹: the installer first offers claude-mem's own hosted note-writer (30-day trial). Your own Anthropic, OpenRouter or Gemini key still sends session data to that provider. 𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗵𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹.
• 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗱: the README's "𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟭𝟬𝘅 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀" has no independent test.
• 𝗖𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗹𝗼𝘁: listed in the repo description, but the repo has no Copilot-specific files as of today.
• 𝗖𝗿𝘆𝗽𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻: the README promotes a third-party token, CMEM, that the author has embraced.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗡𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀

𝗔𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟭𝟭𝟭.𝟴𝗸 𝗚𝗶𝘁𝗛𝘂𝗯 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘀 and 9.7k forks as of today. Created August 2025, Apache-2.0, now at v15.9.0. 𝗔𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟵𝟯𝗸 𝗻𝗽𝗺 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗱𝘀 in the last 30 days.

【Letta、AIが経験を次の課題に生かせるかを測るベンチマークを公開】

AI研究企業のLettaが「FrontierMemory 1.0」を公開した。過去の作業記録から記憶を作り、次の課題に生かせるかを測る。既存のベンチマークを基にした15課題で、作業の決まり、ユーザーの好み、環境の特徴を学ぶ力を調べる。記憶作成は最大6時間。

モデル比較では、記憶を作る仕組み「Letta Dream」と、記憶を使って課題を解くコーディングエージェント「Letta Code」を使用。解答役にはOpus 5.5とGPT-6 Solを使い、考える量の設定を最大にして、2モデルのうち高い達成率を成績とする。

記憶を作るモデルがOpus 5.5またはGLM-5.3なら73.3%、GPT-6.1 SolまたはGemini 4 Argonなら60.0%となった。

Lettaは、Prime IntellectのAIエージェント「Prime Agent」とも比較した。記憶作成と解答にOpus 5.5を最大設定で使い、15課題を各1回解いた達成率は、Letta DreamとLetta Codeの組み合わせが73.3%、Prime Agentが60.0%。

今回の比較では、同じモデルでも、記憶を作って使う仕組みごとに達成率が異なっている。

Meet Letta, a platform for stateful AI agents that keep structured memory and improve across sessions. It is the open-source project behind the MemGPT idea of treating memory as part of the agent runtime.

🧭 Overview
Letta is built for long-running assistants whose identity, facts, and working context must survive beyond one chat window. The repository contains the historical Letta server source; the actively developed agent harness, terminal UI, App Server, channels, and runtime now live in the related Letta Code project.

🛠️ What it does
• Give an agent persistent memory blocks with clear boundaries instead of relying on a short prompt.
• Keep identity, conversation history, and durable state available across sessions and deployments.
• Expose tools and structured outputs so an agent can inspect data, take actions, and update memory deliberately.
• Run locally or self-hosted, with channels for browser, Slack, Telegram, Discord, and custom integrations.

✅ Practical uses
1) Build a personal assistant that remembers preferences without replaying every transcript.
2) Create research or support agents that maintain project facts over weeks of work.
3) Keep memory, identity, and conversations synchronized when an agent moves between devices.
4) Experiment with memory policies, deletion controls, and retention rules before production.

⚙️ Getting started
The current CLI is installed with npm install -g @letta-ai/letta-code. Launch the interactive terminal with letta, or start a local App Server with letta server. Define the memory blocks and tool permissions first, then test what the agent may retain, revise, or delete.

⚠️ License & security
The repository is Apache-2.0 licensed. Treat memory as sensitive state: protect API keys and backups, enforce access controls, set retention and deletion policies, validate tool inputs, and review logs before sharing them.

🔗 Repository: https://github.com/letta-ai/letta
